01 Beam & sample

02 · Gray levels / digitization (optional)

If known, enter the representative open-beam signal per pixel above dark, in camera gray levels (ADU), and the exposure used to measure it. Leave both blank if unknown. For example: 20,000 ADU at 1 s. Use the same detector settings as the scan.

One ADU is one gray-level code. The blank digitization step assumes 1 ADU; blank frame count assumes one reference frame. If the reference is an average, enter the per-frame signal before averaging and the number of frames. Enter the measured intensity, not the number of possible codes (for example, 65,536 for 16-bit data). No gray-level inputs means no quantization estimate.

Standard applications: leave detector & reconstruction calibration blank. Standard planning uses ideal assumptions: k = 1, F = 1, read noise = 0, shared noise floor = 0. This is a planning baseline, not a measured calibration.

03 · Detector & reconstruction calibration — advanced, optional

Leave these fields blank for standard applications. Override only parameters you know from measurements. Each blank field keeps its standard assumption; no calibration values need to be guessed.

Recommended acquisition

Model estimate — not experimentally validated. Standard planning needs no calibration entries and uses ideal noise assumptions. Instrument-specific reconstructed SNR requires measured calibration.

What does “detected neutrons / pixel” mean? The expected number of detected neutron-equivalent events contributing to one pixel during one projection, calculated from flux, pixel area, transmission and detector efficiency. It is a counting-statistics quantity, not the camera gray value. Scintillator/camera systems can produce many gray levels per detected neutron; the conversion is detector-dependent. Gray values are shown separately in ADU when an open-beam measurement is supplied.

SNR ranges · what do they mean?

Here SNR = L/σ, where L is the representative attenuation signal and σ is the modeled reconstructed noise standard deviation. Relative noise is 100/SNR percent of L. The brackets below are illustrative reading aids, not validated image-quality or detection thresholds.

SNR bracketRelative noise (σ/L)How to read it
Below 1Above 100%Noise exceeds the representative attenuation signal.
1 to below 5Above 20%, up to 100%Large fluctuations relative to the signal; substantial uncertainty in individual values.
5 to below 10Above 10%, up to 20%Noise remains a substantial fraction of the signal.
10 to below 20Above 5%, up to 10%Smaller relative fluctuations; suitability depends on the measurement task.
20 to below 50Above 2%, up to 5%A few percent modeled random uncertainty relative to the attenuation signal.
50 and above2% or lessLow modeled relative noise; systematic bias and resolution still need separate checks.

Example: SNR 30 means σ is about 3.3% of L, not 3.3% uncertainty in every physical measurement. High attenuation SNR does not guarantee visibility of a small feature: feature contrast, spatial resolution, artifacts and the reconstruction method also matter. This planner does not calculate feature contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR).

Advanced calibration · optional parameter guide

For standard applications, leave the calibration fields blank. The app supplies the ideal assumptions listed below. This optional step is for users with measurements from the same detector settings, spatial resolution, reconstruction filter and signal/ROI definition as the planned scan. Unknown values should not be guessed.

  • Reconstruction noise gain k (dimensionless; blank → 1): Converts projection noise to the normalized reconstructed attenuation scale. It includes the effect of the reconstruction filter, geometry and noise transfer. A larger k increases predicted noise and usually requires more exposure. Fit it from repeated phantom scans; it is not the camera's electronic gain.
  • Detector excess variance factor F (dimensionless; blank → 1): Multiplies the ideal Poisson counting variance. F = 1 is the ideal counting limit; F > 1 represents additional detector variance. Estimate it from repeated uniform exposures in equivalent neutron counts after accounting for read noise. This model does not allow F below 1.
  • Read noise σᵣ (equivalent detected neutrons RMS per pixel per projection; blank → 0): Independent detector/readout fluctuations added to each projection. Its variance contribution scales as (σᵣ/(qt))², so it matters most at short exposures. Estimate it from repeated dark frames and a measured conversion from ADU to equivalent detected neutrons. Do not enter gray-level RMS directly here. Blank assumes no extra read noise; it does not establish that read noise is absent.
  • Shared reconstructed noise floor σ₀ (normalized attenuation units; blank → 0): A non-averaging noise contribution representing shared flat-field uncertainty, drift or other correlated errors in this simplified model. Longer exposures and more views cannot remove this term. Estimate it from repeat-scan variance over different exposures and projection counts. The combined shared variance is σ₀² + k²v₀ when open-beam quantization v₀ is enabled; its square root sets the SNR ceiling L/√(σ₀² + k²v₀). Avoid counting the same digitization contribution again in a fitted σ₀.
  • Detector efficiency η (percent; default 100%): The fraction of incident neutrons registered as useful detected counts. It sets the count rate, separately from F and read noise. 100% is the requested ideal-efficiency default; replace it with the effective measured value for your detector and neutron spectrum.
  • Effective pixel size p (µm at the sample; default 50 µm): Sets the pixel collection area and detected count rate. It is the sample-plane sampling pitch after magnification/binning, not a measured spatial resolution. The full-period resolution requested in this planner must be at least twice this pitch.
  • Calibration note: Free text included in the exported plan. Record the phantom, date, detector settings, reconstruction filter, ROI/SNR definition and source of the fitted parameters. This note documents provenance; entering it does not validate the model.

If you need an instrument-specific prediction, fit k and σ₀ across multiple N and exposure values, and characterize F and read noise independently where possible. A single scan cannot identify all parameters. Validate on separate scans before treating the estimates as experimentally reliable.

How the estimate works

Resolution convention: r is a full spatial period (two detector samples). Require p ≤ r/2 and N ≥ ceil(πD/r). Angles are 0, 180/N, …, 180 − 180/N degrees; the endpoint is not duplicated.

q = Φ (p × 10⁻⁴)² η T   ·   L = −ln(T)
σ² = k² {[F/(qt) + (σᵣ/(qt))² + vs(t)] / N + v₀} + σ₀²
SNR = L / σ   ·   acquisition time = N(t + overhead)

q is the expected detected neutron-equivalent rate per pixel per second. T and η are fractions. Ideal neutron counts are Poisson (F = 1); F ≥ 1 represents excess detector variance. σᵣ is independent read noise in equivalent detected neutrons per projection. Log-transmission variance uses first-order error propagation.

Optional digitization model: Let I₀ be the dark-subtracted open-beam signal in ADU measured at exposure t₀, Δ the digitization step in ADU, and M the number of independent open-beam frames averaged. Assuming a linear response, sample signal I(t) = I₀Tt/t₀. Uniform rounding error has variance Δ²/12, giving vs(t) = Δ²/[12 I(t)²] for each sample projection and v₀ = Δ²/[12 M I₀²] for the shared averaged reference. The sample contribution averages with N; the shared reference term does not. Both terms are zero when the optional signal/exposure fields are blank.

This rounding approximation assumes independent, sufficiently dithered quantization errors; deterministic or correlated rounding may not average down this way. It excludes clipping, nonlinear/gamma-encoded or display-scaled data, lossy compression, uncertain dark subtraction and Poisson/read noise of the open-beam reference. Use native linear data. An image's bit depth alone does not determine its measured signal or noise. Avoid adding digitization again if it is already included in measured calibration terms. Background: Analog Devices on quantization noise.

The reconstructed signal is a normalized attenuation proxy L. The empirical dimensionless gain k maps projection noise to this signal scale; it is not a universal tomography constant. Shared flat-field, drift and reconstruction errors beyond the optional rounding term are represented by the non-averaging floor σ₀, in the same normalized attenuation units. Reference calibration image acquisition time is excluded.

For every integer N in the allowed range, solve the positive quadratic for the shortest exposure meeting the target; enforce exposure and count bounds, then minimize total time. Equal-time ties choose fewer projections. “Optimal” applies only to this bounded model.

Assumes uniform parallel-beam 180° coverage, a fully covered stationary sample, constant flux, independent views and representative transmission. No scatter, beam hardening, motion, detector MTF, saturation, cone-beam effects or spatially varying attenuation is simulated. Pixel sampling alone does not establish physical resolution. Calibrate and verify with representative phantoms before beamtime decisions.

Background: Kak & Slaney, Principles of Computerized Tomographic Imaging, chapters 3 and 5. The empirical SNR transfer equation here is an explicitly chosen planning model, not a claim from that reference.
